title: Advanced Organic Chemistry
source_note: Standard advanced organic syllabus building on earlier organic chemistry (CHM305) and reaction mechanisms (CHM306): stereochemistry, pericyclic reactions, named reactions, retrosynthetic analysis, protecting groups, heterocyclic chemistry, and modern synthetic methodology.

questions.question: According to the Woodward-Hoffmann rules, a thermal [4+2] cycloaddition (Diels-Alder reaction) proceeds via which pathway?
options: Suprafacial-suprafacial, thermally allowed
Antarafacial-antarafacial, thermally forbidden
Suprafacial-antarafacial, thermally forbidden
It is symmetry-forbidden under all conditions
questions.correct_answer: Suprafacial-suprafacial, thermally allowed
questions.explanation: The Diels-Alder reaction is a thermally allowed [4πs+2πs] pericyclic process under the Woodward-Hoffmann rules, proceeding suprafacially on both the diene and dienophile components.

questions.question: In the Diels-Alder reaction, an electron-rich diene reacts fastest with a dienophile that is:
options: Electron-poor (bearing electron-withdrawing groups)
Also strongly electron-rich
Non-polar and unconjugated
A simple unsubstituted alkane
questions.correct_answer: Electron-poor (bearing electron-withdrawing groups)
questions.explanation: The normal-electron-demand Diels-Alder reaction is fastest when an electron-rich diene (HOMO raised by donor groups) pairs with an electron-poor dienophile (LUMO lowered by acceptor groups such as C=O or NO2), minimising the HOMO-LUMO energy gap.

questions.question: Electrocyclic ring-opening of a cyclobutene under thermal conditions proceeds by which mode of ring closure/opening, per the Woodward-Hoffmann rules?
options: Conrotatory
Disrotatory
Non-rotatory (no bond rotation)
It cannot occur thermally
questions.correct_answer: Conrotatory
questions.explanation: For a 4π-electron electrocyclic process such as cyclobutene ring-opening, thermal conditions dictate a conrotatory motion, whereas the photochemical reaction proceeds disrotatory, as predicted by orbital symmetry conservation.

questions.question: A sigmatropic rearrangement is best defined as:
options: A pericyclic process in which a sigma bond migrates across a conjugated pi system to a new position
The addition of two components across a pi bond to form a ring
The photochemical cleavage of a sigma bond with no bond reformation
A simple SN2 substitution at a carbon centre
questions.correct_answer: A pericyclic process in which a sigma bond migrates across a conjugated pi system to a new position
questions.explanation: Sigmatropic rearrangements (e.g. [3,3]-Cope and Claisen rearrangements) involve concerted migration of a sigma bond from one end of a pi system to the other, with simultaneous reorganisation of the pi bonds.

questions.question: The Claisen rearrangement converts an allyl vinyl ether into:
options: A gamma,delta-unsaturated carbonyl compound, via a [3,3]-sigmatropic shift
An epoxide
A Diels-Alder cycloadduct
A Grignard reagent
questions.correct_answer: A gamma,delta-unsaturated carbonyl compound, via a [3,3]-sigmatropic shift
questions.explanation: The Claisen rearrangement is a concerted [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of an allyl vinyl ether that proceeds through a six-membered transition state to give an unsaturated carbonyl product.

questions.question: Two stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other are called:
options: Enantiomers
Diastereomers
Conformers
Constitutional (structural) isomers
questions.correct_answer: Enantiomers
questions.explanation: Enantiomers are pairs of stereoisomers related as non-superimposable mirror images; they share identical physical properties except for the direction they rotate plane-polarised light and their interaction with other chiral molecules.

questions.question: Diastereomers differ from enantiomers in that diastereomers:
options: Are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other and generally have different physical properties
Are always identical in melting point and boiling point
Cannot exist for molecules with more than one stereocentre
Rotate plane-polarised light by exactly equal and opposite amounts
questions.correct_answer: Are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other and generally have different physical properties
questions.explanation: Diastereomers are stereoisomers (typically arising from molecules with two or more stereocentres) that are not related as mirror images, so unlike enantiomers they have distinct physical and chemical properties.

questions.question: The Cahn-Ingold-Prelog (CIP) priority rules are used to:
options: Assign R/S configuration at a stereocentre by ranking substituents according to atomic number and other defined criteria
Determine the boiling point of a compound
Predict the major product of an elimination reaction only
Calculate the pKa of a functional group
questions.correct_answer: Assign R/S configuration at a stereocentre by ranking substituents according to atomic number and other defined criteria
questions.explanation: CIP rules rank the four groups on a stereocentre by priority (highest atomic number first, then further comparisons outward), and the arrangement of decreasing priority viewed with the lowest-priority group pointing away determines the R or S descriptor.

questions.question: A meso compound is characterised by:
options: Having stereocentres but being achiral overall due to an internal plane of symmetry
Being optically active and rotating light strongly
Having no stereocentres at all
Always existing as a pair of enantiomers
questions.correct_answer: Having stereocentres but being achiral overall due to an internal plane of symmetry
questions.explanation: A meso compound contains multiple stereocentres, but an internal mirror plane makes one half the mirror image of the other, cancelling optical rotation and rendering the whole molecule achiral, as in meso-tartaric acid.

questions.question: In retrosynthetic analysis, a 'disconnection' refers to:
options: The conceptual, imaginary cleavage of a bond in the target molecule to reveal simpler synthetic precursors
The physical breaking of a bond during a real laboratory reaction
The removal of a protecting group
A step that increases molecular complexity
questions.correct_answer: The conceptual, imaginary cleavage of a bond in the target molecule to reveal simpler synthetic precursors
questions.explanation: Retrosynthesis works backward from the target by disconnecting bonds on paper to generate simpler synthons/precursors, guiding the forward synthetic route design.

questions.question: In retrosynthetic terminology, a 'synthon' is:
options: An idealised fragment (often a carbocation or carbanion equivalent) resulting from a disconnection, which must be matched to a real, available reagent
The final isolated product of a synthesis
A protecting group used to mask a reactive functional group
A catalyst used to accelerate a reaction
questions.correct_answer: An idealised fragment (often a carbocation or carbanion equivalent) resulting from a disconnection, which must be matched to a real, available reagent
questions.explanation: A synthon is a conceptual structural unit generated by disconnection; because synthons are often unstable charged species, a real synthetic equivalent (an actual reagent with matching reactivity) is used in practice.

questions.question: Protecting groups are used in multi-step organic synthesis primarily to:
options: Temporarily mask a reactive functional group so it does not interfere with a reaction occurring elsewhere in the molecule
Permanently alter the target molecule's structure
Increase the toxicity of intermediates
Replace the need for purification steps
questions.correct_answer: Temporarily mask a reactive functional group so it does not interfere with a reaction occurring elsewhere in the molecule
questions.explanation: Protecting groups are installed to render a sensitive functional group unreactive under specific reaction conditions and are removed later to reveal the original functionality once no longer needed.

questions.question: A tert-butyldimethylsilyl (TBS) group is commonly used in organic synthesis to protect:
options: Alcohols (as silyl ethers)
Carboxylic acids only
Aldehydes as acetals
Amines as carbamates only
questions.correct_answer: Alcohols (as silyl ethers)
questions.explanation: Silyl protecting groups such as TBS are widely used to convert alcohols into silyl ethers, which are stable to many reaction conditions and can later be removed selectively using fluoride sources such as TBAF.

questions.question: The Grignard reaction involves an organomagnesium reagent (RMgX) reacting with a carbonyl compound to give, after aqueous workup:
options: An alcohol
A carboxylic acid
An alkene
An amine
questions.correct_answer: An alcohol
questions.explanation: Grignard reagents act as nucleophilic carbanion equivalents that add to the electrophilic carbon of a carbonyl group; protonation on aqueous workup gives an alcohol (primary, secondary or tertiary depending on the carbonyl substrate).

questions.question: The Wittig reaction converts an aldehyde or ketone, using a phosphorus ylide, into:
options: An alkene
An alcohol
A carboxylic acid
An epoxide
questions.correct_answer: An alkene
questions.explanation: The Wittig reaction proceeds through a four-membered oxaphosphetane intermediate that collapses to give an alkene and triphenylphosphine oxide, providing a reliable method for controlled C=C bond formation.

questions.question: The Aldol reaction forms a new carbon-carbon bond by:
options: The nucleophilic addition of an enolate (from one carbonyl compound) to the electrophilic carbon of another carbonyl compound
Radical coupling of two alkyl halides
Electrophilic aromatic substitution on a benzene ring
Hydrolysis of an ester
questions.correct_answer: The nucleophilic addition of an enolate (from one carbonyl compound) to the electrophilic carbon of another carbonyl compound
questions.explanation: In the Aldol reaction, an enolate (generated by deprotonation alpha to a carbonyl) attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second aldehyde or ketone, forming a new C-C bond and a beta-hydroxy carbonyl product.

questions.question: The Michael addition (conjugate addition) involves nucleophilic attack at which position of an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound?
options: The beta-carbon (1,4-addition)
The carbonyl carbon directly (1,2-addition)
The alpha-carbon only
The oxygen atom of the carbonyl
questions.correct_answer: The beta-carbon (1,4-addition)
questions.explanation: In a Michael addition, a stabilised nucleophile adds in a conjugate (1,4) fashion to the beta-carbon of an enone, with the negative charge ultimately residing on oxygen before tautomerisation/protonation regenerates the carbonyl.

questions.question: The Fischer esterification mechanism (acid-catalysed reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol) proceeds via:
options: Protonation of the carbonyl, nucleophilic addition of the alcohol, proton transfer, and loss of water to give the ester
A single-step SN2 displacement at the carbonyl carbon
Radical chain substitution
Direct nucleophilic aromatic substitution
questions.correct_answer: Protonation of the carbonyl, nucleophilic addition of the alcohol, proton transfer, and loss of water to give the ester
questions.explanation: Fischer esterification is an acid-catalysed nucleophilic acyl substitution: the carbonyl oxygen is protonated to activate the carbon toward attack by the alcohol nucleophile, followed by proton transfers and loss of water to form the ester.

questions.question: Fischer indole synthesis converts an arylhydrazone of an aldehyde or ketone, under acid catalysis, into:
options: An indole ring system, via a [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement
A pyridine ring
A furan ring
A simple aromatic amine with no ring formation
questions.correct_answer: An indole ring system, via a [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement
questions.explanation: The Fischer indole synthesis proceeds through acid-catalysed tautomerisation of an arylhydrazone to an ene-hydrazine, which undergoes a [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement followed by cyclisation and loss of ammonia to give the indole.

questions.question: Pyridine is an example of a nitrogen-containing heterocycle that is:
options: Aromatic, with the nitrogen lone pair in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, not part of the aromatic pi system
Non-aromatic and fully saturated
Aromatic because its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the ring pi system, like pyrrole
A five-membered ring
questions.correct_answer: Aromatic, with the nitrogen lone pair in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, not part of the aromatic pi system
questions.explanation: Pyridine is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle analogous to benzene; its nitrogen contributes one electron to the pi system (like a ring carbon) while its lone pair sits in an in-plane sp2 orbital, making pyridine weakly basic.

questions.question: Pyrrole differs from pyridine in that pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is:
options: Delocalised into the aromatic pi system, contributing to the ring's 6 pi-electron aromaticity and making pyrrole a much weaker base
Located in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, uninvolved in aromaticity
Absent, because pyrrole nitrogen has no lone pair
Responsible for pyrrole being strongly basic, more so than pyridine
questions.correct_answer: Delocalised into the aromatic pi system, contributing to the ring's 6 pi-electron aromaticity and making pyrrole a much weaker base
questions.explanation: In pyrrole, the nitrogen lone pair is part of the delocalised aromatic sextet, so it is far less available for protonation, making pyrrole a much weaker base than pyridine (whose lone pair is not delocalised).

questions.question: Furan, thiophene and pyrrole are all classified as:
options: Five-membered aromatic heterocycles, each contributing a heteroatom lone pair to a 6 pi-electron aromatic system
Six-membered non-aromatic rings
Fused bicyclic aromatic systems
Saturated cyclic ethers
questions.correct_answer: Five-membered aromatic heterocycles, each contributing a heteroatom lone pair to a 6 pi-electron aromatic system
questions.explanation: Furan (O), thiophene (S) and pyrrole (N) are isoelectronic five-membered aromatic heterocycles in which the heteroatom donates a lone pair into the ring, together with four carbon pi-electrons, to satisfy Huckel's rule (4n+2, n=1).

questions.question: A carbanion intermediate in nucleophilic substitution/addition reactions is generally most stabilised by:
options: Adjacent electron-withdrawing groups that can delocalise the negative charge (e.g. by resonance into a carbonyl)
Adjacent electron-donating alkyl groups
Being located on an sp3 carbon far from any functional group
Increasing steric bulk around the carbanion centre
questions.correct_answer: Adjacent electron-withdrawing groups that can delocalise the negative charge (e.g. by resonance into a carbonyl)
questions.explanation: Carbanions are stabilised by structural features that disperse the negative charge, such as resonance delocalisation into an adjacent electron-withdrawing group like a carbonyl (as in an enolate) or an aromatic ring.

questions.question: A carbene, a key reactive intermediate in organic synthesis, is best described as:
options: A neutral carbon species with only six valence electrons and two non-bonding electrons, typically divalent
A carbon-centred radical with three bonds and one unpaired electron
A carbon bearing a full positive formal charge with three bonds
A stable, isolable closed-shell carbon compound with four bonds
questions.correct_answer: A neutral carbon species with only six valence electrons and two non-bonding electrons, typically divalent
questions.explanation: Carbenes (:CR2) are highly reactive neutral intermediates with a divalent carbon bearing two non-bonding electrons (either paired as a singlet or unpaired as a triplet), commonly generated for cyclopropanation reactions.

questions.question: Singlet and triplet carbenes differ mainly in their reaction stereochemistry because:
options: Singlet carbenes react in a concerted, stereospecific manner, while triplet carbenes react stepwise via a diradical, often losing stereospecificity
Triplet carbenes are always more stable and unreactive
Singlet carbenes cannot undergo cyclopropanation
There is no mechanistic difference between the two spin states
questions.correct_answer: Singlet carbenes react in a concerted, stereospecific manner, while triplet carbenes react stepwise via a diradical, often losing stereospecificity
questions.explanation: Because a singlet carbene has a filled and an empty orbital, it can add to an alkene in one concerted step retaining alkene geometry; a triplet carbene reacts stepwise through a diradical intermediate that can rotate, often eroding stereospecificity.

questions.question: The Baeyer-Villiger oxidation converts a ketone, using a peroxyacid, into:
options: An ester (via oxygen insertion adjacent to the carbonyl)
A carboxylic acid with no change in carbon skeleton
An alkene
An amine
questions.correct_answer: An ester (via oxygen insertion adjacent to the carbonyl)
questions.explanation: The Baeyer-Villiger oxidation inserts an oxygen atom between the carbonyl carbon and one alpha-substituent of a ketone, converting it into an ester (or a lactone from a cyclic ketone), with migratory aptitude determining which group migrates.

questions.question: Asymmetric synthesis techniques (e.g. chiral catalysts or chiral auxiliaries) are used in advanced organic chemistry to:
options: Preferentially produce one enantiomer of a chiral product over the other
Increase the overall yield of a racemic product
Eliminate the need for purification entirely
Convert a chiral starting material into an achiral product
questions.correct_answer: Preferentially produce one enantiomer of a chiral product over the other
questions.explanation: Asymmetric synthesis uses chiral catalysts, reagents or auxiliaries to bias a reaction toward forming predominantly one enantiomer, which is critical since biologically active molecules (e.g. drugs) often require single-enantiomer purity.

questions.question: In the Sharpless asymmetric epoxidation, an allylic alcohol is enantioselectively epoxidised using:
options: A titanium tetraisopropoxide/chiral tartrate ester catalyst with tert-butyl hydroperoxide
A simple peroxyacid such as mCPBA with no chiral induction
Molecular oxygen and a radical initiator
A Grignard reagent
questions.correct_answer: A titanium tetraisopropoxide/chiral tartrate ester catalyst with tert-butyl hydroperoxide
questions.explanation: Sharpless asymmetric epoxidation uses a titanium(IV) isopropoxide catalyst coordinated to an enantiopure tartrate ester ligand with tert-butyl hydroperoxide as the oxidant, delivering the epoxide with high enantioselectivity onto allylic alcohols.

questions.question: Atom economy in the context of modern (green) synthetic methodology refers to:
options: The proportion of the mass of reactants that ends up incorporated into the desired final product
The number of synthetic steps in a route
The total energy consumed during a reaction
The cost of the starting materials only
questions.correct_answer: The proportion of the mass of reactants that ends up incorporated into the desired final product
questions.explanation: Atom economy, a green chemistry metric introduced by Trost, is calculated as the molecular weight of the desired product divided by the sum of the molecular weights of all reactants, favouring routes that minimise wasted atoms.

questions.question: Cross-coupling reactions such as the Suzuki-Miyaura reaction typically form a new carbon-carbon bond between:
options: An aryl/vinyl halide and an organoboron compound, catalysed by palladium(0)
Two identical alkyl halides with no catalyst
An alcohol and a carboxylic acid
Two alkenes via a Diels-Alder pathway
questions.correct_answer: An aryl/vinyl halide and an organoboron compound, catalysed by palladium(0)
questions.explanation: The Suzuki-Miyaura coupling is a palladium-catalysed cross-coupling between an organohalide (or pseudohalide) and an organoboronic acid/ester, proceeding through oxidative addition, transmetalation and reductive elimination to form a new C-C bond.

questions.question: In nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on an aryl halide, the reaction is facilitated by:
options: Strong electron-withdrawing groups (e.g. NO2) positioned ortho or para to the leaving group, which stabilise the anionic Meisenheimer intermediate
Electron-donating groups such as -OCH3 ortho/para to the leaving group
The complete absence of any substituents on the ring
A strongly acidic reaction medium
questions.correct_answer: Strong electron-withdrawing groups (e.g. NO2) positioned ortho or para to the leaving group, which stabilise the anionic Meisenheimer intermediate
questions.explanation: SNAr proceeds through an anionic (Meisenheimer) intermediate that is stabilised by resonance delocalisation of negative charge onto electron-withdrawing substituents positioned ortho or para to the site of attack, accelerating the reaction.

questions.question: Which named rearrangement converts an amide into a primary amine with loss of one carbon, via an isocyanate intermediate, using a hypohalite?
options: Hofmann rearrangement
Beckmann rearrangement
Curtius rearrangement
Claisen rearrangement
questions.correct_answer: Hofmann rearrangement
questions.explanation: The Hofmann rearrangement (Hofmann degradation) treats a primary amide with bromine (or another halogen) and base to generate an isocyanate intermediate that hydrolyses to a primary amine with one fewer carbon than the starting amide.

questions.question: The Beckmann rearrangement converts a ketoxime, under acidic conditions, into:
options: An amide, via migration of the group anti to the leaving hydroxyl
A nitrile
An alcohol
An alkene
questions.correct_answer: An amide, via migration of the group anti to the leaving hydroxyl
questions.explanation: In the Beckmann rearrangement, protonation/activation of the oxime hydroxyl triggers departure of water with concomitant migration of the substituent anti-periplanar to the leaving group, ultimately giving an amide (industrially used to make caprolactam from cyclohexanone oxime).
